newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine job accident insurance firms eye mergers.
newsitem.headline: Argentine job accident insurance firms eye mergers.

text.p: After three months of business, Argentina's private work accident insurance firms (ARTs) are already studying mergers to survive tough competition in a crowded market, market sources say.
"The tendency to consolidate will be very strong in Argentina. It's clear that 40 ARTs are too many," said Jorge Ferrari, general manager of the Omega insurance firm.
Ricardo Romanelli, president of ART Liberty, said 10 players would suffice. "There will be mergers. The current situation is unsustainable," he said.
At present five of the country's 44 ARTs control 46.83 percent of the market share of 3.65 million workers.
The ARTs are legally allowed to regroup as from January.
"Now is the time for strategy and planning. I think (mergers) will start in the first quarter of 1997 and maybe pick up between March and June," Ferrari said.
Omega and Provincia are the leading ARTs, grouping 12.11 percent and 11.14 of workers, respectively, followed by Asociart, La Caja and Consolidar.
Jorge Garcia of the firm La Buenos Aires said ARTs insuring between 20,000 and 40,000 workers "will find it very difficult to operate based on their income. I'd say 100,000 is the starting point."
Chile, with a workforce less than half the size of Argentina's, has only three ARTs while in Spain the market is 20 percent larger but has only 20 insurance firms.
"Companies with many less than 100,000 clients have no purpose, unless for some reason they are working in a niche in which they are really efficient," said Romanelli.

Before starting up operations last July Argentina's ARTs had estimated the market worth at $1.2 million yearly, but the actual number is closer to $500 million or less than the estimated insurance payouts of $750 million.
"ART losses in the first year will be around $400 million," said Romanelli.
The cost of insuring a worker in Argentina is 1.5 percent of his salary, against 2.4 percent in Chile, 2.6 percent in the United States and 2.8 percent in Spain.
